title: Bottom-Up AI Design of Selective Calcium Ion Channels From Scratch
whyItMatters: First bottom-up AI design of selective transmembrane calcium ion channels built from scratch—opening programmable control over electrical signaling in living cells.
summary: Published in Nature in October 2025 by Yulai Liu, Connor Weidle, Ljubica Mihaljević, and David Baker at the University of Washington Institute for Protein Design, researchers used deep-learning protein design (RFdiffusion, ProteinMPNN, and AlphaFold) to build transmembrane calcium-selective ion channels from defined selectivity-filter geometries completely from scratch. Patch-clamp electrophysiology and cryo-EM confirmed that the AI-designed nanopores assemble inside lipid membranes, match atomic models accurately, and selectively conduct Ca²⁺ ions over competing monovalent ions such as Na⁺.
technicalHighlights: Designed transmembrane pore architectures directly around idealized ion-coordinating selectivity filters rather than modifying natural channel scaffolds.
Single-channel electrophysiology confirmed robust conductance and selective Ca²⁺ permeation over monovalent ions, matching cryo-EM structural reconstructions.
Demonstrated bottom-up synthetic control over membrane proteins central to cardiac, neural, and intracellular electrical signaling.
caveats: First-generation de novo channels lack the complex voltage-sensing and ligand-gating regulatory domains of natural mammalian calcium channels.
institutions: University of Washington (Institute for Protein Design)

scoreRationale.foundational: Extended generative protein design into one of structural biology’s hardest frontiers: ion-selective transmembrane channels.
scoreRationale.ripple: Opens synthetic electrophysiology, biosensing nanopores, and programmable cellular signaling therapeutics.
scoreRationale.verification: Peer-reviewed in Nature (648: 468–476) with cryo-EM structures and functional patch-clamp electrophysiology.
scoreRationale.velocity: Achieved selective ion-channel synthesis bottom-up without relying on natural membrane-protein templates.
